# Decisions and tries {#decisions-and-tries}

## The gap {#gap}

*I've decided* sounds final even when you could still change your mind, and *I'll try* sounds like a hedge even when you are committed to trying. Neither *I've decided* nor *I'll try* says how settled you are. In Ageben, the ending on a decision word or a try word says how settled the decision is or how committed the try is.

## The forms {#forms}
<!-- Agent summary: two sets of drop-ins. Decision `thogel` / `thogem` / `thoger`: you have made a choice to do the act; does not say the act happens. Try `howal` / `howam` / `howar`: the act is attempted; says nothing about whether it works. Placement: where English puts an adverb or tag, usually the end of the clause; covers its clause. Unsure → middle one: `thogem` (can still change; claims nothing about how firm the choice will turn out), `howam` (commitment unsaid). Omit the decision word when only saying the act happens (plain *We're moving to Denver*). -->

The drop-ins in this lesson come in two sets of three. A **decision** word says that you have made a choice to do the act. A **try** word says that someone attempts the act, and it says nothing about whether the attempt works.

| Drop-in | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `thogel` / `thogem` / `thoger` | have decided: for good / and can still change it (the default) / for now |
| `howal` / `howam` / `howar` | try: until it works or is ruled out / with the commitment unsaid (the default) / as a trial run |

Put the drop-in where English would put an adverb or a tag, usually at the end of the clause. Wherever it goes, it applies to the whole clause it sits in.

When you can't tell which ending fits, use the middle one. `thogem` says you have decided and can still change your mind, and it is also the form to use when you don't know how settled the decision is. How firm a choice will turn out is hard to know even about your own choices, so `thogem` claims nothing either way. `howam` says that you try and leaves out how committed you are.

Leave the decision word out when you are only saying what happens. *We're moving to Denver* with nothing added says that the move happens. *We're moving to Denver `thogel`* says that you have decided for good to move, and it does not claim that the move happens.

## What the ending says {#endings}
<!-- Agent summary: endings follow the settled-to-passing scale from *How sure are you?*: `-l` lasting, `-m` the default, `-r` right now; each word gives them its own meaning. Decision = how final: `thogel` for good, `thogem` can still change, `thoger` for now only; the verb stays the same. Try = how committed: `howal` keeps trying until it works or is ruled out, `howam` unsaid, `howar` a trial run, a low-stakes probe that plans for failure (if it fails, finding that out was the point). Use `howar` to lower the stakes of starting, for yourself or someone else. -->

The endings `-l`, `-m`, and `-r` are the three from *How sure are you?*, where they run from most settled to most passing. Think of `-l` as *lasting*, `-m` as the default in the middle, and `-r` as *right now*. Each word gives the three endings its own meaning along that line.

### On a decision {#on-a-decision}

On a decision word, the ending says how final the decision is. Here is one choice with each ending:

> We're selling the car `thogel`.  
> We're selling the car `thogem`.  
> We're selling the car `thoger`.

With `thogel`, you have decided for good, and the choice is final. With `thogem`, you have decided and can still change your mind. With `thoger`, the decision holds for now only. Because the ending carries how open the choice is, the rest of the sentence stays the same in all three.

### On a try {#on-a-try}

On a try word, the ending says how committed the attempt is, meaning how far you will go with it. Here is one attempt with each ending:

> I'm learning to swim `howal`.  
> I'm learning to swim `howam`.  
> I'm learning to swim `howar`.

With `howal`, you are committed: you will keep trying until you can swim or until it is ruled out. With `howam`, you are trying, and how committed you are is left unsaid. With `howar`, it is a trial run, a small probe such as a few lessons to see how it goes.

A trial run plans for failure. If the lessons don't work out, finding that out was the point of the probe. So use `howar` when you want to lower the stakes of starting something, for yourself or for someone else.

## Examples {#examples}

> I'm going vegetarian `howar`.  
> We're moving to Denver `thogel`.  
> I'm taking the job `thogem`.  
> I'm learning piano `howal`.  
> We're skipping the party `thoger`.

*We're moving to Denver `thogel`* says the decision to move is final. *I'm taking the job `thogem`* says you have chosen the job and could still change your mind. *I'm going vegetarian `howar`* is a trial run: if the diet does not suit you, finding that out was the point.

## Telling them apart {#telling-apart}
<!-- Agent summary: near misses. Decision vs plan (*Wants and plans*): plan word = you mean to do a later act, ending = how far it is worked out; decision word = a choice made and how readily you would change it, whenever the act falls (fits before you start and while you do it). Both: plan word first (`thagom` `thogel`). Decision vs promise: `thogel` is a choice only you can see; a promise is a yes given openly that others can hold you to; no drop-in here, so *I promise* stays English. Try vs result: plain sentence = the act happens; try word = the attempt happens, outcome open; omit it when saying the act happened. A try word makes no claim about whether you can (ability suffix, *Can and can't*). Whose: decision word = your decision, even when someone else does the act; someone else's decision stays English. Try word = whoever does the act tries. -->

Four cases are easy to confuse with these drop-ins, and each is handled differently.

### A decision or a plan {#decision-or-plan}

*Wants and plans* taught the plan word, which says that you mean to do an act and how far the plan is worked out. A plan is about an act that still lies ahead. A decision word says that you made the choice and how readily you would change it, whenever the act falls, so it fits both before you start and while you are already doing it.

For example, *I'm working from home `thagom`* says that you mean to work from home and have the steps laid out. *I'm working from home `thogem`* says that you have chosen to, and it is true whether you start next month or are at your desk now.

To say both how far the plan is worked out and how firm the decision is, use both words, with the plan word first. *I'm working from home `thagom` `thogel`* says the steps are laid out and the choice is final.

### A decision or a promise {#decision-or-promise}

A decision made for good is still a private choice. *I'm walking to work `thogel`* reports a final decision that only you can see. With *I promise to walk to work*, you give a yes openly, and others can hold you to it. This lesson has no drop-in for a promise, so make a promise in plain English.

### A try or a result {#try-or-result}

A plain sentence says that the act happened. *I fixed the sink* says the sink is fixed. *I fixed the sink `howam`* says you made the attempt and leaves open whether it worked. So when the sink is fixed and you are saying so, leave the try word out.

A try word also makes no claim about whether you are able to do the act. For that, use the ability suffix from *Can and can't*, which says whether someone can do something or which kind of *can't* applies.

### Whose decision, whose try {#whose}

A decision word means your own decision, even when someone else does the act. For example, *the kids go to bed at eight `thogel`* says that you have decided for good that the kids go to bed at eight. These drop-ins cannot say what someone else decided, so keep that in English: *Sam decided to stay*.

A try word works differently: it means that whoever does the act makes the attempt. *The kids are learning to swim `howal`* says that the kids will keep trying until they can swim or it is ruled out.

## Practice {#practice}

Add the drop-in that fits the note.

**1.** *I'm quitting coffee.* (only a trial)

::: details Show answer
I'm quitting coffee `howar`.
:::

**2.** *I'm quitting coffee.* (you'll keep trying until it works or is ruled out)

::: details Show answer
I'm quitting coffee `howal`.
:::

**3.** *We're selling the house.* (decided for good)

::: details Show answer
We're selling the house `thogel`.
:::

**4.** *We're selling the house.* (decided, and you could still change your mind)

::: details Show answer
We're selling the house `thogem`.
:::

**5.** *I'm staying home tonight.* (decided for now)

::: details Show answer
I'm staying home tonight `thoger`.
:::

**6.** *I'm staying home tonight.* (you'll try to, and you aren't saying how hard)

::: details Show answer
I'm staying home tonight `howam`.
:::
